# Factoring & Solving Quadratics

<p class="demo-subtitle">A short, self-checking course module built entirely with
Quarto and the <code>math-exercise</code> extension — no server, no LMS,
just a browser. This page shows one coherent teaching sequence end to end:
exercise → hint → worked solution → follow-up → assessment.</p>

<div class="demo-hero-meta">
<span>🧮 SymPy-checked answers</span>
<span>🌐 Runs fully client-side (Pyodide)</span>
<span>💬 Progressive AI hints</span>
<span>🔁 Randomized task pools</span>
</div>
:::

This module targets a first bridging-course topic: **factoring and solving
quadratic equations** via the difference-of-squares pattern and general
trinomials. Every exercise below is a live, working `math-exercise` block —
try it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this module, a student can:

- expand and factor simple quadratic expressions,
- solve a quadratic equation by factoring,
- apply a quadratic model to a numeric question, and
- recognize the same pattern across problems of increasing difficulty.
:::

---

## 1 · The exercise {#sec-warmup}

::: {.demo-step-head}
<span class="demo-step-num">1</span>
<span class="demo-pill demo-pill-feature">✓ math-exercise capability: `mode: equivalent` + `form: expanded`</span>
:::

A student opens the module and meets the first task. Any algebraically
equivalent answer is accepted, but it must actually be **expanded** — typing
the un-multiplied product back is correctly rejected as "not in the
requested form."

```{math-exercise}
#| label: warmup
#| caption: Warm-up — expand a product
#| vars: x
#| mode: equivalent
#| form: expanded
Expand the product: $(x-3)(x+3) = $ __[x**2 - 9]
```

## 2 · Stuck? Ask for a hint {#sec-hints}

::: {.demo-step-head}
<span class="demo-step-num">2</span>
<span class="demo-pill demo-pill-feature">✓ math-exercise capability: built-in progressive AI feedback</span>
:::

Every exercise on this page already has a **Feedback** button (next to
Check, above). It calls any OpenAI-compatible model — Cerebras, OpenRouter,
OpenAI, a local Ollama — configured once per browser, and the hint gets
**more concrete each time the same student asks again on the same task**:

| Attempt | What the tutor says |
|---|---|
| 1st click | A gentle nudge — the solution is *not* given away |
| 2nd click | A concrete hint about the solution approach |
| 3rd+ click | The full step-by-step solution |

::: {.callout-note}
For a live demonstration, click **Feedback** on the exercise in
[§1](#sec-warmup) after entering a (possibly wrong) answer. This needs an
API key for the chosen provider — several offer a free tier (see the
[README](../README.md#ai-feedback)). Screenshots of this dialog and the
resulting hint bubble are good candidates for the funding application.
:::

## 3 · The worked solution {#sec-solution}

::: {.demo-step-head}
<span class="demo-step-num">3</span>
<span class="demo-pill demo-pill-showcase">🧩 demo presentation — standard Quarto callout, not an extension feature</span>
:::

Instead of (or alongside) AI feedback, a course can simply publish the
worked solution as ordinary Quarto content — here as a collapsible callout,
directly below the matching exercise:

```{math-exercise}
#| label: factor
#| caption: Now go the other way — factor it
#| vars: x
#| mode: equivalent
#| form: factored
Factor the expression: $x^2 - 9 = $ __[(x-3)*(x+3)]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 📖 Show worked solution

$x^2 - 9$ is a **difference of two squares**: $a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b)$.

Here $a = x$ and $b = 3$, since $9 = 3^2$. Substituting:

$$x^2 - 9 = x^2 - 3^2 = (x-3)(x+3)$$

Notice this is exactly the reverse of the expansion in
[the warm-up exercise](#sec-warmup) — the two tasks are the same identity,
read in opposite directions.
:::

## 4 · A related follow-up {#sec-followup}

::: {.demo-step-head}
<span class="demo-step-num">4</span>
<span class="demo-pill demo-pill-feature">✓ math-exercise capability: `mode: set` and `mode: numeric`</span>
:::

Two follow-ups build on the same identity: first *solving* the equation
(multiple correct answers, order-independent), then *applying* the same
kind of expression to a numeric, real-world question.

```{math-exercise}
#| label: solve
#| caption: Solve it
#| vars: x
#| mode: set
Solve $x^2 - 9 = 0$. Give all solutions, comma-separated: __[3, -3]
```

```{math-exercise}
#| label: applied
#| caption: Apply it — a quadratic model
#| mode: numeric
#| tolerance: 0.1
A stone is thrown so that its height after $t$ seconds is
$h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t$ metres.
What is its height at $t = 1.5\text{ s}$, in metres?
$h(1.5) = $ _[18.75] m
```

## 5 · Practice variants {#sec-variants}

::: {.demo-step-head}
<span class="demo-step-num">5</span>
<span class="demo-pill demo-pill-feature">✓ existing feature</span>
<span class="demo-pill demo-pill-vision">🔮 envisioned extension</span>
:::

Two different ideas about "variants," shown side by side and kept
deliberately distinct.

### 5a · Task pools — an existing capability

`math-exercise` already supports a **task pool**: a set of hand-authored
variants of the same problem, one shown at random per browser session, with
a reload button (top-right of the box) to draw a new one.

```{math-exercise}
#| label: pool-factor
#| caption: Practice pool — click ↻ for a new random variant
#| vars: x
#| mode: equivalent
#| form: factored
#| pool: true

Factor: $x^2 - 16 = $ __[(x-4)*(x+4)]

---

Factor: $x^2 - 36 = $ __[(x-6)*(x+6)]

---

Factor: $x^2 - 49 = $ __[(x-7)*(x+7)]
```

::: {.callout-important}
**This is real, working functionality** — the three variants above are
written directly in the document; `math-exercise` picks and remembers one
per session and swaps it in on reload. No AI involved.
:::

### 5b · Difficulty progression — an illustration, not a feature

<span class="demo-pill demo-pill-vision">🔮 future vision — hand-written here to stand in for AI generation</span>

The three tasks below are **written by hand for this demo**. They illustrate
what an AI question-generation step could plausibly hand a course author —
several variants of the *same underlying concept* at increasing difficulty —
which the author would then drop into `math-exercise` blocks exactly like
any other exercise. `math-exercise` itself does not generate exercises; it
only renders and checks whatever content it is given.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%"}
<span class="demo-level-badge demo-level-1">Level 1 · easier</span>

```{math-exercise}
#| label: level1
#| caption: Difference of squares
#| vars: x
#| mode: set
Solve: $x^2 - 4 = 0$ __[2, -2]
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
<span class="demo-level-badge demo-level-2">Level 2 · medium</span>

```{math-exercise}
#| label: level2
#| caption: Trinomial, integer roots
#| vars: x
#| mode: set
Solve: $x^2 - x - 6 = 0$ __[3, -2]
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
<span class="demo-level-badge demo-level-3">Level 3 · harder</span>

```{math-exercise}
#| label: level3
#| caption: Leading coefficient ≠ 1
#| vars: x
#| mode: set
Solve: $2x^2 - 3x - 2 = 0$ __[2, -1/2]
```
:::

::::

## 6 · Assessment & progress {#sec-progress}

::: {.demo-step-head}
<span class="demo-step-num">6</span>
<span class="demo-pill demo-pill-feature">✓ per-exercise: strict, symbolic correctness checking</span>
<span class="demo-pill demo-pill-showcase">🧩 dashboard below: demo-only illustration</span>
:::

Assessment already happens **inside every exercise above**: each `Check`
click runs a real symbolic comparison in SymPy, not string matching — it can
require a *specific algebraic form* (factored, expanded, exact, reduced),
not just a numerically correct value. That is what makes `form: factored`
above reject a mathematically-correct-but-unfactored answer.

What `math-exercise` does **not** currently provide is a course-wide view
across many exercises. The panel below is a small demo-only script
(`assets/progress-tracker.js`, ships only with this demo) that watches the
pass/fail state `math-exercise` already puts on the page and aggregates it —
illustrating what a lightweight course dashboard or gradebook feed could
look like.

::: {.callout-warning}
The panel below is **not** part of `math-exercise`. It is presentation code
specific to this demo, built only on the extension's already-public DOM
output (the `math-input-ok` / `math-input-wrong` classes it adds after a
check). No extension file was modified to build it.
:::
